extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / general literate English public interested in manners, fashion, and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Short early-18th-century periodical essays (The Spectator) giving moral reflections, social criticism, prescriptive rules for behaviour, fashion, and conversation for the polite English reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in female ornamentation / head-dress
rubrics_metrics.description: The author urges women to 'consider how impossible it is for them to add any thing that can be ornamental to what is already the Master-piece of Nature' and criticises excessive head-dress (Fontanges) that 'destroy the Symmetry of the human Figure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the Fontange (tall cone/spire structures) as an extravagance that makes a woman appear like a 'Colossus'; cites historical reaction (Thomas Conecte preaching, women burning head-dresses, mob pelting wearers). Advises prevention by recommending moderation while fashion is against excess; argues that nature already beautifies the head (face, hair, eyes) so supernumerary ornaments only 'call off the Eye from great and real Beauties to childish Gewgaws.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of honour: courage for men, chastity for women
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement: 'The great Point of Honour in Men is Courage, and in Women Chastity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains rationale: each sex values the quality that renders them most amiable to the opposite sex; notes social consequences (a man's honour may be regained by another encounter, a woman's 'slip' is 'irrecoverable'); contrasts with alternative possible choices (wisdom, wit). Uses examples from chivalry and national manners (Spain, romances) to illustrate how these ideals shape behaviour and fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calling someone a liar is the chief violation of honour
rubrics_metrics.description: The author asserts that 'The great Violation of the Point of Honour from Man to Man, is giving the Lie' — calling another a liar is an affront that 'nothing but Blood can expiate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains psychological reason: accusing someone of lying is tantamount to calling them a coward because lying implies lack of courage; supports with Herodotus' Persian educational ideal 'to speak Truth.' Shows how this belief fuels duelling culture and false notions of honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject false notions of honour that contradict law or religion
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'the Dictates of Honour are contrary to those of Religion and Equity, they are the greatest Depravations' and should be 'exploded by all Governments.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates active suppression of pernicious honour codes (e.g., duelling); proposes public punishments (pillory) to disgrace duelists as a deterrent; contrasts honour that 'runs parallel with the Laws of God and our Country' (which should be cherished) with honour that promotes wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate a disposition to be pleased / good-humour as duty
rubrics_metrics.description: It is 'the Duty of every Man that would be true to himself, to obtain... a Disposition to be pleased' and to place himself 'in a constant Aptitude for the Satisfactions of his Being.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticises affected delicacy, valetudinarians (those who constantly complain of ailments), indolence, and an over-attentiveness to others' 'false pleasures.' Praises persons (e.g., Varilas) who by temperament cheer and enliven company even without memorable witticisms. Advises avoiding sourness and cultivating cheerfulness so that 'there are no Moments lost.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dominating conversation with personal complaints or ailments
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay condemns those who 'entertain those with whom they converse by giving them the History of their Pains and Aches' as offering 'the meanest Help to Discourse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advises that mutual good humour is a proper 'Dress' for company; one should speak of matters that cause friends to rejoice rather than complain about personal health. If one is too weak to bear ordinary company pleasures, one should 'keep his Chamber.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Make conversation pleasant: present others in their best light
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for conversation that shows everything 'in its Excellence' rather than in 'its Degeneracy' — 'Beautiful Pictures are the Entertainments of pure Minds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that company is more agreeable when speakers avoid shocking topics and are 'apt to set [things] in the best Light.' Implies choosing pleasant topics, avoiding malicious representations, and a charitable tone toward subjects discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and plainness in speech; avoid hollow compliments
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity is praised and 'the great and general Want of Sincerity in Conversation is none of the least' faults of the age; excessive compliments amount to 'a Prostitution of Speech.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Tillotson: modern conversation is 'swelled with Vanity and Compliment' so words become 'meer Cyphers.' Argues it is better to be what one would seem than to counterfeit excellence (it's as troublesome to maintain a pretence as to have the virtue). Encourages natural plainness, abhorrence of pomp in compliments, and an honest style suited to the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dissimulation: practical cost of falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissimulation brings 'an everlasting Jealousie and Suspicion' so that 'he is not believed when he speaks Truth, nor trusted when perhaps he means honestly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that once a man 'hath once forfeited the Reputation of his Integrity, he is set fast' and that both truth and falsehood will thereafter fail to serve him. Encourages long-term investment in integrity to preserve credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical judgment should prefer temporal distance / posterity
rubrics_metrics.description: The author argues that 'It is therefore the Privilege of Posterity to adjust the Characters of illustrious Persons' because living partisans prevent impartial assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that contemporaries are biased by friendships and enmities; only after passions subside and rivalries end can historians 'make an impartial Distribution of Fame.' Uses imagined future historian evaluating the reign of Anne to illustrate fair reassessment of fame and genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give indulgence when reading older writers / interpret archaic styles charitably
rubrics_metrics.description: We must 'make Allowance for the Mirth and Humour of the Author' and show 'indulgence which we must shew to old English Writers' for obsolete words and obscure allusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that literal reading of old texts leads to absurd conclusions (e.g., women passing whole mornings at puppet-shows); advises interpreting remote hints as allusions to then-fashionable follies now obscure. Encourages contextual reading rather than literal modern judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social charms: combine imagination, good breeding, and sweet disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'well-corrected lively Imagination and good Breeding' added to 'a sweet Disposition' make one of the greatest social blessings, qualifying a person to 'communicate' cheerfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Varilas as example: he contributes to company not by memorable witticisms but by innate temper and manner; the combination attracts universal welcome. Implies that social value is as much temperament and manners as wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fan-exercise: 'Handle your Fans' (basic salute/ready position)
rubrics_metrics.description: First word of command: 'Handle your Fans' — shake the fan with a smile, tap the right-hand woman, press lips with the fan's extremity, let arms fall and stand ready.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as the basic motion, done with a closed fan and generally learned in the first week of training; part of the regimented 'Exercise' for mastering fan etiquette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fan-exercise: 'Unfurl your Fans' (display & vibrational motions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Command 'Unfurl your fans' includes little flirts, vibrations, gradual openings, and voluntary fallings-asunder in the fan—revealing pictures (Cupids, Garlands, Altars, Birds, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This motion 'pleases the Spectators more than any other' and typically takes about a month's practice to learn; it displays decorative figures and is a public show-quality movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fan-exercise: 'Discharge your Fans' (loud crack)
rubrics_metrics.description: Command 'Discharge your Fans' is a collective loud 'crack' like a pocket-pistol; one of the most difficult parts of the exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trainer instructs on proper occasions for using the crack to prevent misuse; notes technical innovations (fans with enclosed wind) can amplify sound so even a young girl can make a loud report. Emphasises controlled, appropriate use (avoid letting off fans in wrong places).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fan-exercise: 'Ground your Fans' (graceful disarming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Command 'Ground your Fans' teaches a lady to quit her fan gracefully (toss aside to take up cards, adjust hair, replace pins, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This movement consists in tossing a fan with an air upon a long table and may be learned in two days or in a year depending on attention; it's practical for polite behaviour when moving from one activity to another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fan-exercise: 'Recover your Fans' (quick, composed retrieval)
rubrics_metrics.description: Command 'Recover your Fans' trains ladies to catch up their fans in a hurry and place themselves in proper station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not difficult if the lady applies herself; part of the coordinated drill where the regiment is momentarily disarmed and then must resume positions gracefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fan-exercise: 'Flutter your Fans' (expressive master-movement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Fluttering of the Fan' is the master-piece of the exercise: many varieties (angry, modest, timorous, confused, merry, amorous) correspond to emotions; 'scarce any Emotion in the Mind does not produce a suitable Agitation in the Fan.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mastery typically takes about three months (teacher lays aside dog-days/hot summer time for training); by observing a disciplined fan one 'knows... whether she laughs, frowns, or blushes'; author has compiled 'The Passions of the Fan' and offers instruction to gentlemen in 'the whole Art of Gallanting a Fan.'
